result.markdown: --- title: "Data-to-decision capstone" course-unit: ch15-data-to-decision-capstone status: complete --- ## From committed data to a conditional decision The capstone makes each transition inspectable: **provenance → model choice → fit → residuals → parameter envelope → scenario** - Eight committed Eyam observations, 18 June–20 October 1666. - $N=261$ is the modeled population at the second-wave start. - No render-time data download; the notebook has a deterministic fallback. ::: {.notes} This is an educational workflow, not a new historical reconstruction. The data and caveats are documented in data/README.md and the TOML provenance file. ::: ## Model and data caveats We fit an effective transmission rate $\lambda=\beta c$ and removal rate $\gamma$: $$ \dot S=-\lambda SI/N,\qquad \dot I=\lambda SI/N-\gamma I,\qquad \dot R=\gamma I. $$ The state columns are reconstructed from historical records and assumptions, not direct measurements. A homogeneous closed SIR model omits rodent-to-human transmission, household structure, movement, and reporting changes. ::: {.notes} The effective lambda is deliberately not interpreted as separate contact and per-contact transmission parameters; the sensitivity and identifiability chapter explains why. ::: ## Verify locally, then fit ```julia metadata = TOML.parsefile("data/eyam_plague_1666.toml") data = CSV.read("data/eyam_plague_1666.csv", DataFrame) @assert bytes2hex(sha256(read("data/eyam_plague_1666.csv"))) == metadata["csv_sha256"] @assert all(data.S .+ data.I .+ data.R .== metadata["population"]) loss(θ, _) = sum(((predict(θ) .- observed_states) / metadata["population"]) .^ 2) fit = solve(OptimizationProblem( OptimizationFunction(loss, AutoFiniteDiff()), [1.0, 0.5], nothing; lb = [1e-4, 1e-4], ub = [8.0, 8.0]), Fminbox(LBFGS())) ``` The normalized all-state least-squares objective is transparent, but it is not a count likelihood. ## Fit diagnostics and deterministic envelope ::: {#cell-fig-slide-ch12-fit .cell execution_count=1} ::: {#fig-slide-ch12-fit .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` Committed Eyam states, a fitted SIR trajectory, and residuals. ::: ::: Retaining nearby $\pm10\%$ parameter combinations gives a **scenario envelope**, not a calibrated confidence interval. ::: {.notes} Residual patterns are evidence about model mismatch, not just optimizer quality. With eight reconstructed rows, formal uncertainty needs an explicit observation model. ::: ## Decision comparison Add $C$ with $$ \dot C=(1-v(t))\lambda SI/N. $$ Compare no policy with a one-month 50% reduction beginning at month 1, and propagate the accepted parameter envelope through both scenarios. - Validate $S+I+R=N$, finite trajectories, and lower modeled final incidence under the policy. - Interpret the result as a model-based counterfactual under the chosen assumptions. ::: {.notes} The final comparison is decision-relevant only after its assumptions, parameter envelope, and data limitations are stated alongside it. ::: ## Takeaways and next steps - A checksum verifies bytes, not historical truth. - $\lambda$ is an effective rate; it does not identify $\beta$ and $c$. - Residuals and sensitivity determine what conclusions are defensible. - Better decisions require better observation and mechanistic models. Read the [capstone chapter](../../chapters/15-data-to-decision-capstone.html), [data provenance](../../data/README.html), and the [CSV.jl](https://csv.juliadata.org/stable/) and [Optimization.jl](https://docs.sciml.ai/Optimization/stable/) documentation. ::: {.notes} Invite learners to replace one assumption at a time: an observation model, household structure, or a different decision objective. The workflow should survive that replacement even when the SIR model does not. :::
